\section{Results}\label{sec:5}\ThesisCheckNumber{section}{5}

Every table in this section is taken directly from the authoritative, validated output files listed in Appendix A; no coefficient was computed for this chapter. Coefficients are reported with 95\% confidence intervals, except in Table 5.4, which reports coefficients and p-values only. P-values are shown to three decimal places when the underlying value is at least .0005 and as ``\textless.001'' when it is smaller. Both forms are display precision only; the full-precision value of every cell is stored in the authoritative output files. Where a model has two inference conventions, both are labelled explicitly (Section 4.5), and the prose uses the primary convention unless the sensitivity convention is named.

Household water and sanitation are entered together in every model in Table 5.1 (Sections 4.1, 4.2). No household coefficient reaches significance \textbf{at the 5\% level} in the cluster-fixed-effects specification, this thesis's main household result and the one least exposed to cluster-level confounding; water--HAZ (\emph{p} = .062) does cross the 10\% threshold, stated explicitly rather than left implicit. Non-significance is read as inconclusive, not as proof no association exists --- the water--HAZ interval, for example, spans −0.175 to +0.004. Under the more conservative FULL\_DUMMY\_DF sensitivity (Section 4.5), the cluster-FE p-values are .080 (water--HAZ) and .574 (sanitation--HAZ), the same substantive conclusion. These use the normal reference distribution the baseline pipeline's code actually computes (Section 4.5), not the Student \emph{t}(\emph{G}−1) distribution used for the historical extension (Section 4.6).

The community water and sanitation coefficients, which are entered together at every stage (Section 4.3), are large and highly significant before adjustment. They attenuate sharply as socioeconomic status and region fixed effects are added, and neither is significant at the fully adjusted stage. \textbf{This attenuation pattern is consistent with confounding by local socioeconomic conditions, but it does not, on its own, establish confounding as the sole explanation}; a change in measurement structure as controls absorb variance, or other coinciding specification features, could produce the same pattern. The same four-stage pattern holds for WAZ and WHZ, except that the WHZ water association is already small and statistically insignificant before adjustment (0.033, \emph{p} = .545) and remains so throughout. Across all three outcomes, the fully adjusted specifications (the community models here and the household models in Table 5.1) do not show a consistent association between improved WASH and child anthropometric outcomes, at either level --- read as ``this sample does not provide clear evidence of an association once the obvious confounders are controlled,'' not as ``WASH has no true relationship with child growth,'' a materially stronger claim than this design can support.

One cell in this table reaches significance at the 5\% level: household water for HAZ, conditional on community water and the other two WASH terms (β = −0.085, \emph{p} = .043), and its sign is unexpectedly negative. The result is therefore reported as a single finding rather than treated as a central conclusion of this thesis, and it is not interpreted as evidence that improved household water is harmful.

The Nigeria community sanitation--HAZ coefficient changes sign and grows in absolute size as controls are added sequentially, from 0.274 with no controls to −0.457 once socioeconomic controls are included. A block-by-block audit finds that removing wealth quintile alone from the full control set moves the coefficient from −0.457 back to −0.196, the largest movement produced by any single control block. This demonstrates sensitivity to specification; it is not proof that wealth is the specific mechanism behind the reversal. The corresponding household-level (cluster-fixed-effects) coefficient for Nigeria is close to zero and not significant. This instability is reported as evidence that the community-level, region-fixed-effects estimate for Nigeria sanitation is \textbf{not stable across specifications}, and it should not be read as evidence that improved sanitation harms child growth in Nigeria.

\subsection{Current-age heterogeneity}\label{sec:5.5}\ThesisCheckNumber{subsection}{5.5}

In the heterogeneity models, six current-age bands (0 to 5, 6 to 11, 12 to 23, 24 to 35, 36 to 47, 48 to 59 completed months) replace the continuous age control, 12--23 months as reference (Section 4.4). Of twelve exposure-specific joint interaction tests (two exposures × three outcomes × two fixed-effects structures, each a \(\chi^2\) test of five restrictions), \textbf{eleven of twelve reject the null of no heterogeneity} at the 5\% level (the exception: the water interaction for WHZ under region fixed effects, \emph{p} = .300); the combined ten-term tests (\(\chi^2\), 10 df) reject in all six combinations (largest \emph{p} = .019). The household-WASH association with current outcomes therefore varies with current age in most specifications tested. As Section 4.4 states, this is secondary evidence about the \emph{current} survey-date association only --- it compares children of different current ages at one survey date, and does not trace growth over time or reconstruct any child's actual early-life exposure, a question addressed only by the historical extension below, under its own separate limitations.

\subsection{Historical extension: primary established-date models}\label{sec:5.6}\ThesisCheckNumber{subsection}{5.6}

All cells below come from the primary weighted models with the post-12-month window, estimated on the established-date sample (Ghana 2014, Kenya 2014, Nigeria 2018). Coefficients are per 10 percentage points of IHME-modelled local coverage. The exposure is an area average of the modelled coverage surface within each child's buffer; it is neither the source study's population-weighted aggregate nor a record of the child's own household facilities (Section 3.5). The estimates are weighted conditional associations among eligible measured children, not population-representative estimates (Section 3.8). Their confidence intervals and p-values use the Student \emph{t}(\emph{G}−1) reference distribution (Section 4.5). Every cell carries the same methodological qualifications, stated in Section 3.8 and discussed fully in Section 6, and none is promoted above the others for being significant.

The pooled established-date water--HAZ coefficient (1.03, \emph{p} \textless{} .001) is this section's selected headline, the cell this thesis discusses in most depth. It is \textbf{not} the only nominally significant cell among the 24 shown above. At conventional \emph{p} \textless{} .05, \textbf{six} of the 24 cells reach significance: pooled water--HAZ, pooled water--WAZ, Ghana water--HAZ, Nigeria water--HAZ, Nigeria water--WAZ (\emph{p} = .0498) and Ghana sanitation--HAZ, the last in an unexpected negative direction. The displayed, rounded \emph{p} = .050 for Nigeria water--WAZ in Table 5.5 should not be read as lying exactly at the threshold, because the underlying value is below .05. The pooled water--HAZ cell was chosen as the headline because it is the pooled, established-date estimate for this thesis's primary outcome and primary window, a choice made before any coefficient was examined (Section 6.4), not because it is the only significant result. A reader comparing the tables with this text should therefore see six significant cells, not one.

All 24 primary cells in Table 5.5 and Table 5.6, including this headline, were independently reconstructed and re-estimated with a different estimation library on a separately rebuilt sample, matching the stored coefficients, standard errors, confidence intervals and p-values (Appendix B.2). This establishes that the reported numbers are what the documented specification, correctly implemented, actually produces --- it is \textbf{not} a multiplicity correction: no formal adjustment for testing 24 cells has been applied, so the check does not make this result, or its five other nominally significant siblings, any less likely to reflect chance given the number of cells examined, and it does not establish causality.

\textbf{Weighted vs.~unweighted, same observations.} The pooled water--HAZ coefficient is sensitive to the equal-country weighting convention. It is 1.03 when weighted (equal country totals) and 0.41 {[}0.03, 0.80{]}, \emph{p} = .035, when unweighted on the identical 23,018 observations. This is a disclosed, authorised sensitivity to a stated design choice (Section 4.5), not evidence that either weighting is more ``correct'', and both are reported together whenever this coefficient is cited. Equal country weight totals do not give each country equal influence on the pooled slope, which also depends on each country's residual exposure variation (Section 4.5). Neither the weighted nor the unweighted estimate is a population-representative estimate (Section 3.8).

\textbf{Residual exposure variation and the 10-point scale.} The pooled water--HAZ model's residual within-cluster exposure standard deviation after all controls is 0.43 percentage points. The conventional 10-percentage-point coefficient scale is therefore roughly 23 times larger than the exposure contrast that actually identifies the model. One residual standard deviation of exposure corresponds to approximately 0.044 HAZ standard deviations. The 10-point coefficient should therefore be read as a reporting convention for comparability across studies, not as a description of a change that is typically observed within a cluster.

\subsection{Alternative windows and common-sample comparison}\label{sec:5.7}\ThesisCheckNumber{subsection}{5.7}

The historical pipeline estimates 291 models in total: the 24 primary established-date cells of Section 5.6, their unweighted counterparts, and several further sensitivity families --- alternative exposure windows, wealth adjustment, spatial-assignment method, completion-rule strictness, calendar-age construction, Ethiopia's provisional candidates, and DHS/IHME overlap exclusions (full counts in Appendix C). To avoid repeating every cell, only the pooled water--HAZ cells are shown below as the headline case; the corresponding sanitation and WAZ/WHZ sensitivity cells are neither more nor less favourable to a WASH association (most show the same wide, zero-spanning intervals as Section 5.6) and are available in full in the project's output tables, omitted here for brevity, not because water--HAZ happened to be significant.

The first four rows each use their own window's eligible sample, so differences between them reflect differences in samples as well as in windows; only the last row holds the sample fixed. The post-12-month estimate changes from 1.03 on its own eligible sample to 1.64 on the smaller common sample eligible under all four windows. This is a \textbf{sample-composition effect} (children with complete 24-month windows differ systematically from the full post-12-month sample), not evidence favouring the validity of one window over another. No window was selected because of the significance of its coefficient; all four are reported together, as planned before any coefficient was examined (Appendix C).

\begin{ThesisTableNote}

\emph{Note.} Coefficients are per 10 percentage points, as in Table 5.5. The row excluding Ghana pools Kenya and Nigeria only, and is not an overlap-free estimate: Kenya's own DHS survey also feeds into the IHME water product used as its exposure (Section 6.5), so excluding Ghana removes only one of the two established-date countries with this input overlap; every other row uses the three-country established-date sample.

Adding wealth leaves the coefficient essentially unchanged (1.01 vs.~1.03). This shows only that the reported conditional coefficient is not sensitive to this particular adjustment. It does not establish that wealth mediates the historical WASH exposure, and a small change under adjustment is not itself evidence against the competing possibility that wealth is a confounder the main specification should have included. Section 3.8 states both the mediator concern and this competing concern, and this sensitivity adjudicates neither. Nor does it, on its own, support or contradict a cluster-fixed-effects absorption mechanism, which this thesis's own baseline model separately demonstrates is not how cluster fixed effects behave (Section 4.2). The spatial-method and completion-rule sensitivities move the coefficient by amounts smaller than, or comparable to, the gap between the main weighted and unweighted estimates, and none of them is privileged over the main specification.

\subsection{Ethiopia: provisional, excluded from the established-date pooled sample}\label{sec:5.9}\ThesisCheckNumber{subsection}{5.9}

Ethiopia's three interview-date candidates are not treated as equally valid sensitivity evidence. Candidate C1 uses a 30-day Ethiopian-calendar arithmetic conversion that has already been shown, independently of the WASH analysis, to be invalid for the delivered recoded date fields (Appendix C). It is excluded from this section and from every reporting table, and its past numerical agreement with the other two candidates is not treated as evidence of robustness. Candidates C2 and C3 remain provisional, since neither has been independently validated. They agree closely with each other (water--HAZ: −0.39 for both; sanitation--HAZ: −0.45 for both; all four confidence intervals include zero). These estimates are reported here and in Appendix C only as an explicitly exploratory sensitivity analysis. They are never pooled into, or compared with, the established-date headline results above.
